To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the fraction of star-forming disks is steadily declining over time, (2) the fraction of quenching spheroids is steadily rising, (3) the fractions of both star forming spheroidal and quiescent disk dominated galaxies are approximately constant, and (4) the model is successful at reproducing some of the observed trends, but not the relative fractions of the four quadrants.

the fraction of spheroid-dominated quiescent galaxies increases steadily over cosmic time, and the fraction of star-forming disk-dominated galaxies decreases steadily, while the fractions of quiescent disks and star-forming spheroids stay nearly constant.
the fractions of quiescent and disk-dominated galaxies both increase with time, while the fractions of star forming and spheroid galaxies remain approximately constant.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of the morphological mix of galaxies over cosmic time.
the morphological evolution of galaxies and the physical processes that drive this evolution.
how galaxies form their spheroids (bulges) and how they quench their star formation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evolution of the galaxy population is qualitatively well reproduced by our semi-analytic framework, but that the details of the physical processes that drive this evolution remain unclear.

semi-analytic modelling can successfully describe the evolution of the main population, but that there are still some discrepancies with the observed fractions of star forming and quiescent galaxies with spheroid-dominated morphology, and that the relative importance of the physical processes driving morphological transformation and star formation quiescence are still not fully understood.
the evolution of the galaxy population is reasonably consistent with the predictions of the model, but there are some dierences in the details that require further study.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the observed quiescent fraction and the relative fractions of the four quadrants in the SFR-Sersic plane are reproduced by a semi-analytical model that includes both major and minor mergers as well as disk instabilities as mechanisms for bulge growth, although the model predicts a stronger decline of the star forming spheroid population than observed, and a larger increase of quiescent disks.

semi-analytic galaxy evolution models can qualitatively reproduce the observed evolution in the quiescent fraction, but that more detailed studies are required to fully understand the evolution of the star forming fraction and the relative fractions of the different types.
the evolution of the galaxy population is broadly consistent with the idea of a “downsizing” of star formation and bulge growth, but the details are not yet well constrained.
The main takeaway from our work is that

semi-analytic galaxy evolution models, with reasonable assumptions about bulge growth and feedback, can reproduce the evolution of the overall morphological distribution of galaxies, and the buildup of spheroid-dominated and quiescent galaxies, but the details of the model can have significant impact on the predicted fractions of star forming disks, quiescent sphericoids, and star forming spheroid-dominated objects.

the observed evolution of the quiescence and spheroid fractions can be reproduced by a model with bulge growth via mergers and disk instability, and AGN feedback via mergers and a disk instability driven superwind.
a model with a single channel for spheroid growth (either mergers or disk instabilities) is unable to simultaneously reproduce the evolution in the fractions of all four subpopulations.
